description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): éeḍi; Morphemic form: aḍ-
family_analysis: Palula áaḍu is early and root-accented before final u. This fits the extended-nominal pattern and subsequent root-a lengthening after rdh reduction. Because the old dictionary also points to árdha, this family is not an unambiguous demonstration of accent reset from an exclusively oxytone ancestor.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): éemi; Morphemic form: áam-
family_analysis: Palula óomu and Biori úumu have early root accent and retain the final gender vowel. This is diagnostic for accent assignment to a long root before extension: the long ā then undergoes Ashret/Biori raising. Copying final accent from āmá would not predict the early raised root. The independently attested āmaka formation makes extension substantially better grounded here than a suffix supplied only from modern u.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): aawíiṛi
family_analysis: Palula aawíiṛu and Strand awʹiṛo both accent the final root syllable before the gender vowel, despite old initial ā́. The shift cannot be simple attraction to an inherited long vowel because the old second nucleus is vocalic r. An extended-adjective accent rule predicts the locus, while quantity differs between the primary modern sources. Covered or enclosed to narrow/tight is semantically plausible.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): uthéeli; Morphemic form: uthál-
family_analysis: Palula utháalu has early prominence on the final long root syllable before u, a clear modern member of the root-final adjective class. Old variants differ in root quantity and final consonant and lack independently recorded accent. The modern class assignment is supported by adjective morphology, but historical retraction cannot be measured from these unaccented inputs.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): ungúri; Morphemic form: ungúr-
family_analysis: Modern Palula ungúru and Gilgit hagúro/agúro accent the final root syllable before a gender ending, while older Palula úguro/úṅguro is initially accented. This is a real source or historical formation discrepancy within a well-defined adjective class. Sauji ugəró has a finally accented vowel and must be checked for its exact inflection; Kalkoti ugur/uɣur has lost the ending.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): úbi; Morphemic form: ub-
family_analysis: Palula úbu ‘light in weight’ has initial short-root prominence before an unaccented ending after strong contraction and shortening. The source's elevated-to-light semantic proposal is possible but not transparent, and the old participle lacks an accent here. The modern adjective fits a short monosyllabic-root class without proving that the proposed old word is its unique source.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): úči; Morphemic form: uč-
family_analysis: Palula úču ‘few, a little’ has initial short-root prominence before an unaccented ending, fitting the modern adjective class. The old reconstructed ō has shortened and changed quality, and its accent is unrecorded. The source associates the word with a broader defective/small expressive family, limiting the certainty of a unique inherited input.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): khéeči; Morphemic form: khač-
family_analysis: Palula číčal ‘mud’ has initial short prominence and extra l-bearing formation, whereas kháaču ‘bad’ belongs to an adjective class and is duplicated under *kacca ‘raw’. Kundal cical is a useful cognate without marked accent; Sauji khaco concerns the adjective. The distinct lexical formations and competing etymologies must be retained separately.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): khúši
family_analysis: Palula khúšu ‘left’ has short root prominence before a gender ending, while Gilgit košóli ‘broken bowl, shards’ has an additional accented derivative. Aspiration and sibilant variation may reflect expressive or borrowed layers.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): kriṣíṇi; Morphemic form: kriṣíṇ-
family_analysis: Palula kriṣíṇu/kiṣíṇu has accent on the final root syllable before u, while Shina kíṇo/kíṇu has only one root syllable after greater cluster reduction. Thus the modern first-versus-second syllable difference is predicted by root shape plus the same extension rule; it is not divergent inherited accent. The independently attested old extended adjective strengthens the morphological analysis.

family_analysis: Palula koomáalu and Strand komʹâlu accent the final root syllable and leave the older initial long o unaccented. This supports root-final accent assignment in an extended adjective; it is not quantity attraction to the first long vowel. The aa in the accented open root syllable can be secondary lengthening of old short a.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): khúṭi
family_analysis: Palula khúṭu and Gilgit khúro both accent a short root before a gender ending, but their consonants select different independently recorded variants of the defective/lame family. The old short/long variants are unaccented, so the consistent modern adjective pattern is stronger evidence than a unique historical accent input.

gloss: big, large; grown, old; great; adult (man), elder
description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): géeḍi; Morphemic form: gaḍ-
family_analysis: Palula gáaḍu ‘big, old’ has early long-root prominence before u, while baaugáaṛu ‘shoulder’ is an arm-plus-thick compound. The compound's accent on the second constituent is not an independent reflex of the simplex as a whole word. Unraised aa raises a chronological question if the vowel is inherited long and early; alternative geminate or later-lengthening histories must be independently established.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): ghaḍeerí; Morphemic form: ghaḍeer-; Variant restriction: Biori
family_analysis: Biori ghaḍeerú and Ashret ghaḍeeró/gaḍheeró older accent the final gender vowel, unlike ordinary gáaḍu big. Liljegren2016Table7.4p153 explicitly pairs them with younger lhookeeró/ú and identifies both as older comparative formations. The independently attested gāḍhatara4119 comparison therefore supports a morphological class with ending accent, not an exceptionless rule for all short-u adjectives. Older gaḍhḗro has stem accent, so the cross-source trajectory remains unresolved.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): ghéeni; Morphemic form: ghan-
family_analysis: Liljegren gháanu is early root-accented in the extended big adjective, compatible with open-syllable short-a lengthening. Strand ghâʹnu is late in the same apparent formation. The modern u/ee feminine alternation supports an inflectional formation, but does not remove the source disagreement. Sauji ghaṇyeṛo has extra derivation and cannot be counted as the same stem.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): čúkri; Morphemic form: čukr-
family_analysis: Palula čúkru and Gilgit čúrko share root prominence before the gender vowel, against final-accented cukrá. Their kr/rk difference is metathesis within the root; it does not itself shift accent. The attested old extensions support morphological reaccentuation. The plant names with final ī are different derivatives and must not enter the adjective's outcome cell.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): čuṇi; Morphemic form: čuṇ-
family_analysis: Palula and Shina čúṇu/čúno share short root prominence before an unaccented ending despite old long ū. The minute/pulverized-to-small meaning is independently supplied, and the adjective-class accent is consistent. Root shortening is a separate historical problem; the unaccented old input cannot resolve it or prove a particular reaccentuation.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): ǰéendi; Morphemic form: ǰand-
family_analysis: Palula ǰáandu is early-root-accented, and the old source already supplies barytone jī́vant as an alternative to final-accented jīvantá. Gilgit ǰoóno is late long, while ǰiino is unmarked. Contraction of īva and cluster reduction produce different root vowels, so this family cannot simply be scored as retained or shifted from the first headword.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): téeti; Morphemic form: tat-
family_analysis: Astori tátto preserves a geminate stage that links old pt reduction to the other dialects. Kohistani táto/Guresi tátu are short, Gilgit taáto is late long, and Palula táatu is early long. A common root-accented extended adjective followed by dialect-specific geminate treatment explains both shared locus and divergent mora alignment: preservation, simplification without lengthening, compensatory late lengthening, or a later Palula open-syllable lengthening layer.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): tíiṇi; Morphemic form: tíiṇ-
family_analysis: Palula tíiṇu and the four Shina tíiṇo/tíiṇu forms have early long root accent before their gender ending, against old final accent. Retention of old long ī while kṣṇ simplifies makes this a strong extension example with little vowel-alignment ambiguity. Kalkoti tiin adds segmental coverage but no reliable tone in the older unmarked source.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): triṣṭi; Morphemic form: triṣṭ
family_analysis: Palula tríṣṭu and Strand trʹisṭo preserve the root cluster and have root accent before o/u; Gilgit c̣íṭo has stronger cluster reduction. The extended-adjective rule predicts the locus in both. Some modern Gilgit forms are also linked to tiktá, so the old consonant history must decide between them; accent alone cannot.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): deec̣híṇi; Morphemic form: deec̣híṇ-
family_analysis: Palula deec̣híṇu and Shina dac̣híno/daṣínu all accent the final root syllable before the gender ending, although the old adjective is initially accented. The agreement survives different initial-vowel qualities and affricate histories. Because the old later vowel was short, this cannot be explained by attraction to a pre-existing long vowel; it is a diagnostic extended-stem accent case.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): dhrígi; Morphemic form: dhríg-
family_analysis: Palula dhrígu and Shina ẓígo/j̣ígu have short root accent before the gender vowel, against the old final-accented adjective. Root-final accent assignment explains locus, while old ī shortening before the rg(h) history is independently required. Newer Kalkoti dríg has H associated with final-vowel loss, whereas the older unmarked drig is not itself evidence of no H. Kundal drī̌g is another distinct quantity outcome.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): néeni; Morphemic form: nan-
family_analysis: Palula náanu and Gilgit náno are root-accented before their gender vowel, agreeing with independently attested barytone nágnaka rather than the simple final-accented adjective. Palula long aa versus Gilgit short a then reflects different quantity history after gn simplification. Sauji niċaṅ requires separate suffix/consonant analysis and is unmarked.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): néewi; Morphemic form: naw-
family_analysis: Palula náawu is early while Gilgit naáwo is late on a long vowel before a preserved w and gender ending. Kohistani nóo~, Guresi náa~ and Astori náu~ have early root prominence with different contraction. Gilgit's late aa therefore cannot be attributed to loss of the visible w alone; a historical extended-stem or geminate/glide stage is needed. This is a stringent residual for a cluster-only account of new late vowels.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): níili; Morphemic form: níil-
family_analysis: Palula níilu and Schmidt/Degener Shina níilo/níilu preserve early root accent on old long ī. Buddruss niílo ‘blue’ is late in an otherwise comparable Gilgit adjective. Since the root was already long, this cannot be explained as the new short-vowel cluster compensation seen in ‘hot’. It is a direct source/lexical variation test for the early-long baseline.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): paṇéeri; Morphemic form: paṇár-
family_analysis: Palula paṇáaru has early accent on the final root syllable before u, while the old principal adjective is initially accented. Old later a was short, so extension-driven root-final accent plus open-syllable lengthening predicts the modern locus and new aa; old first ā has shortened. Kalkoti pänär and Sauji parãṛó represent additional vowel and ending histories. The old alternate pāṇḍurá must remain visible.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): puréeṇi; Morphemic form: puráaṇ-
family_analysis: Palula puróoṇu/Biori purúuṇu and Gilgit puróono have early accent on the final root syllable before the gender ending, against old final accent. description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): bhúuri; Morphemic form: bhóor-
family_analysis: Palula bhúuru ‘deaf’ has early long root prominence before u, but buuḍóolu ‘spider’ accents a later extended root syllable; Gilgit taṛabúulo has still more material. These are distinct formations within a loose expressive family. The deaf lexeme is also linked under 9530 and 9633 and must not count three times.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): búuḍi
family_analysis: Palula búuḍu/Strand bʹûḍo has early long root prominence before the gender ending. Turner explicitly argues that initial b across languages excludes direct derivation from vr̥ddhá and offers contamination or a br̥h-related alternative. Importing vr̥ddhá's accent to create a late-to-early exception would ignore that independent segmental objection.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): bhakúli; Morphemic form: bhakúl-
family_analysis: Palula bhakúlu has short prominence on the final root syllable before u and an independently visible ul extension. Kohistani bhaák ‘bull’ instead has late aa in a closed monosyllable, compatible with a new-long aspirated environment but not directly the same formation. Lump-to-fat and lump-to-bull are separate semantic derivations.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): bhúuri; Morphemic form: bhóor-
family_analysis: Palula bhúuru has early long prominence before u and is the same deaf lexeme also grouped under 9268 and 9633. The different reconstructed roots are alternatives within a broad defective-word family, not independent supporting cases. The modern adjective can be classified morphologically while historical input uncertainty remains explicit.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): mhoóri
family_analysis: Palula mhoóru has late prominence on its long root before an unaccented u; older mohóro retains evidence for the contracted medial syllable. Its root-final accent locus is compatible with the extended adjective pattern, but its late mora is not the early mora of tíiṇu or puróoṇu. Contraction of multiple old syllables and aspiration relocation provide independent conditioning to test rather than forcing all u-final adjectives into one contour class.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): yúuṛi
family_analysis: Palula yúuṛu and Strand yʹûra have early long root prominence with different gender or number endings. The immediate nominal *yōṭa, not the broad verb *yuṭati, is the relevant input. Turner explicitly calls derivation from yuta/yuktá phonetically difficult, so importing yuktá's accent would bypass a known segmental objection.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): lhoóki; Morphemic form: lhoók-
family_analysis: Palula lhoóku and Gilgit loóko have late long-root accent before an unaccented gender vowel, while older lohóko preserves a less contracted stage. This parallels madhurá > mhoóru: root-final accent is compatible with the adjective class, but mora alignment differs from early tíiṇu. Loss/reorganization of medial aspiration and contraction provide independently visible conditions for a late subclass.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): aaghaabéeni
family_analysis: Palula aaghaabáanu ‘sky-coloured’ is a compound, with accent in the colour constituent and an unaccented adjective ending. It therefore cannot be compared with várṇa as though the entire modern word were a simple sound reflex. The short old a and lost r also make the modern aa a later quantity development; its early alignment is compatible with root-final adjective accent in a monosyllabic second constituent.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): bidréegi; Morphemic form: bidrág-
family_analysis: Palula bidráagu ‘sick’ has early long prominence in the final root syllable before u, fitting the extended adjective pattern. Strand budrag- is a verbal stem ‘be sick’ and is not the same accent cell. The unusual reconstructed compound and dh/r/g developments need independent support, despite the plausible motionless-to-ill semantic path.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): bíiḍi; Morphemic form: bíiḍ-
family_analysis: Palula bíiḍu/Strand bʹîḍo has early long root prominence before a gender ending after prefix and cluster reduction. The grown-to-much semantic path and participial formation independently motivate the class. The whole prefixed input is unaccented; the accent of bare vr̥ddhá cannot be substituted without justification.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): bistíiṇi; Morphemic form: bistíiṇ-
family_analysis: Liljegren bistíiṇu has early long ii before u; Strand bistʹiṇo has the same root-syllable placement but short i. The inherited long ī and rṇ cluster give independent structural controls. The quantity difference is a source or dialect issue requiring verification and must not be silently normalized away.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): šidéeli; Morphemic form: šidál-
family_analysis: Palula šidáalu and Gilgit šidálo accent the final root syllable before an unaccented gender vowel, with western long versus Gilgit short a. Gilgit/Kohistani šaál ‘fever’ instead has a contracted late-long monosyllabic form and a different grammatical category. Both the retained adjective ending and the noun's contraction are independent conditioning features; the pair must not be collapsed into an irregular single outcome.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): šišáwi
family_analysis: Palula šišáwu/šišówo accents the final root syllable before an unaccented gender ending, while the old reduplicated form was initially accented. This supports morphological reaccentuation of an adjective, but the w and changed vowel grades require an actual stem history. Sauji ṣoṣ ‘summer’ is a reduced seasonal noun with no secure mora marking and should not be treated as the same adjective cell.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): ṣíiṛi; Morphemic form: ṣeéṛ-
family_analysis: Palula ṣíiṛu/Strand ṣʹîṛo has early long root prominence before u/o, whereas Sawi séṛo has short initial prominence. The old source entertains several competing defective or broken-root analyses, including contamination. Modern agreement in root placement supports a morphological class but cannot choose the proto-root or its accent.

description: Inflection: Uml (Fem): séetri; Morphemic form: satr-
family_analysis: Palula sáatru/Strand sʹâtru has early long initial prominence before u. The old asylum/abode meaning does not directly mean low, so a building-related semantic derivation needs explanation. Long sārtra and short sattra alternatives also prevent a unique quantity history from being assumed solely because the modern root is long.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): šišáwi
family_analysis: Palula šišáwu has short prominence on the final root syllable before u, while older šišówo means clean. The prefix plus splendid formation independently motivates an extended adjective, and w reflects medial consonant history. Parent śōbhā́ is a different noun; its final accent cannot simply be treated as the whole adjective's input.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): c̣húuṇc̣i; Morphemic form: c̣húuṇc̣-
family_analysis: Palula c̣húuṇc̣u and Gilgit súu~c̣o have early long root prominence before gender endings; Strand's c̣hu~c̣- is a derived straighten stem. Turner explicitly proposes a connection with sū́kṣma, making old barytonesis a conditional, independently stated hypothesis rather than a certainty. The unusual initial affricate and nasal-cluster development remain crucial.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): síndi; Morphemic form: sind-
family_analysis: Palula síndu/Strand sʹindo has initial short-root prominence before the gender ending and retains a voiced nasal cluster. The reconstructed wet participle and its relation to tintá should be kept explicit; an accent from another branch cannot automatically be transferred. This is a short-root extended adjective control.

description: Inflection: Reg (Fem): thúli; Morphemic form: thul-
family_analysis: Palula thúlu has short root prominence before an unaccented gender ending, consistent in locus with the extended adjective class but with shortening of old ū. Kundal ṭʰūl ‘egg’ is semantically and phonologically distinct; it may be a separate derived or contact word and cannot count as the adjective's direct accent outcome merely because the DB links it here.
